slides.heading: Count Inversions
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Very Hard · Sorting
slides.narration: Let's solve Count Inversions, a very hard sorting problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Number of pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j], counted during merge sort.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Number of pairs i under j with a i over a j , counted during merge sort.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Merge sort counts inversions: when a right element is placed before remaining left elements, they all form inversions.
slides.narration: Merge sort counts inversions: when a right element is placed before remaining left elements, they all form inversions.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Merge sort counting → O(n log n)
BIT over values → O(n log n)
slides.narration: Checking all pairs is quadratic. Counting during merge sort is n log n.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 2. During merge, add remaining left count when taking from the right
slides.narration: Step by step. First, sort halves recursively. Second, during merge, add remaining left count when taking from the right. Third, sum.

slides.caption: Count cross inversions while merging
slides.narration: While merging, each time a right element goes before remaining left elements, those left elements each form an inversion with it.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: Count recursively sorts both halves, copies to aux, and merges; when taking from the right, it adds mid minus i plus one.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n log n. Space is O of n.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
slides.narration: Take from the left on ties so equal values aren't counted.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Merge sort counts inversions: when a right element is placed before remaining left elements, they all form inversions.
